text: We partnered with Baseten to build the largest-scale harness leaderboard using 83B tokens across 27,280 agent runs. We wanted to answer two questions: when you switch your model, should you consider switching the harness too? What is the best harness for each model? Previously, our v1.0 FrontierHarness leaderboard ranked harnesses on a single model, Kimi K3. V1.1 expands the benchmark to 22 harnesses × 5 models × 62 tasks × 4 attempts, 76× the size of v1.0. Through our experiments, we found that you should consider switching harnesses when switching models to maximize your experience. Each model had a different best-value (pass rate vs. cost) harness: Codex CLI with GLM-5.3, Pi with GLM-5.3 Flash, ZCode with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, Oh My Pi with Muse and Alma with Kimi-K3. Cost ranks moved far between models. By cost per task, the median harness moved 11 of 22 places, and Codex CLI went from 1st with GLM-5.3 to 16th with Kimi-K3. Figure 1. Cost per task and pass rate of each harness Each point is one harness: further left is a lower average cost per task, and higher is a higher pass rate. The orange line joins the harnesses that no other harness beats in both cost and pass rate. Select a model to filter all figures of this post. Over all models, four harnesses are on the line: OpenCode v2 (lowest cost per task, $0.561), Pi, Codex CLI and ZCode (highest pass rate, 61.9%). The others cost up to 1.6 times as much and passed 50.6% to 60.2%. Each card names the best-value harness for one model: the lowest cost per pass, unless another harness costs at most 30% more per pass and passes at least 5 points more often. This rule picked ZCode over OpenCode v1 with DeepSeek (25% more cost, 7.7 more points) and Alma over Oh My Pi with Kimi-K3 (9% more cost, 6.5 more points). V1.0 ran nine harnesses with one model. Their pass rates were within 17 points of each other, but the median cost per pass differed by 17 times. We thought that this came mostly from the pair of harness and model: a harness that is cheap with one model can be expensive with another. V1.1 runs each harness with five models. Harnesses. 18 harnesses. The four DeepSeek Harness profiles have different tool sets, and OpenCode ran at two versions. Each counts separately: 22 configurations. Table 2 in the appendix gives their versions. Models. Baseten served all five: GLM-5.3 ( zai-org/GLM-5.3 ), GLM Flash ( zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash ), DeepSeek ( deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 ), Muse ( meta-models/muse-spark-open ) and Kimi-K3 ( moonshotai/Kimi-K3 ). Tasks. 62 terminal tasks. The time limits are those of the tasks, from 15 minutes to 8 hours. We ran the Harbor evaluation with each harness’s default settings, because we think this is closest to how people use a harness every day. Each harness used the same version and settings with all models, at the maximum reasoning effort. Figure 2. Methodology A cell is one harness and model pair. We use the two cost metrics of our dashboard : We pick the best value by cost per pass because we want harnesses at the top left of a chart of pass rate against cost per task: a high pass rate at a low cost. Draw a line from the origin to the point of a harness. Its slope, pass rate ÷ cost, is the passes per dollar. Cost per pass is the inverse of this slope, so the lowest cost per pass has the steepest line. Audits of the trial logs flagged 216 trials for reward hacking, and 163 of them were online lookups. These trials score 0. Table 3 in the appendix gives the count for each harness and model. Figure 3. Cost and pass rate of each harness with each model A deeper cell costs less than the others in its column. Codex CLI was the cheapest per pass with GLM-5.3, $0.803, but 12th with Muse and 10th with Kimi-K3. Over all models, it cost the least per pass, $0.937, and Antigravity CLI the most, $1.63. We drew the 62 tasks again 4,000 times and chose the best-value harness each time. Codex CLI stayed first with GLM-5.3 in 99.6% of the draws. The other four winners are the most likely of several close harnesses: Oh My Pi with Muse (53%), ZCode with DeepSeek (47%), Pi with GLM Flash (42%) and Alma with Kimi-K3 (25%). The model sets the general level of the cost, because the list prices of the models differ by 20 times or more (Figure 9). We took the average cost per task of the 110 cells on a log scale, so that a doubling counts the same with each model. A two-way analysis of variance divides the spread of these costs into three parts: So with the model fixed, 68% of the variation between harnesses (4.9 of 7.2 points) depends on the pair, or is noise. Figure 4. Lowest-cost and highest-cost harness for each model Each row is a model, on a log scale of average cost per task. The ratio divides the highest cost by the lowest. To test for chance, we shuffled the trials between the harnesses of each model 300 times and calculated the ratio again. “Chance” is the median of these ratios, 1.2 to 1.8 times. All five real ratios are larger than every shuffle (p = 0.003), so the spread comes from the harnesses, not from the noise of reruns. The largest is with DeepSeek: Cline CLI cost 5.0 times as much as OpenCode v1, for 2.0 more points. With the other models, the cheapest harness per task was at most 0.4 points behind the most expensive one. Figure 5. Cost rank of each harness with each model (1 = lowest cost per task) Each line is a harness, with the cheapest at the top. The five highlighted lines are the cheapest harnesses per task with GLM-5.3, GLM Flash, DeepSeek, Muse and Kimi-K3. Codex CLI was 1st with GLM-5.3 and 16th with Kimi-K3. DeepSeek Harness: Creator moved the most, from 1st with Muse to 21st with GLM Flash. OpenCode v1 was 1st with DeepSeek and 13th with Muse. Reruns do not explain these moves. We divided the attempts into two halves and ranked the harnesses by cost in each half. With the same model, the two rankings had a mean rank correlation of 0.71. With two different models, it was 0.26. Figure 6. Lowest and highest cost per pass for each model This is Figure 4 for cost per pass. After each ratio is the rank correlation of the cost per task and the pass rate of the harnesses, from −0.39 to +0.22. A positive value means that the more expensive harnesses passed more often. The harness with the highest pass rate was 5th to 20th of 22 in cost per task. With four of the five models, the most expensive harness per pass passed less often than the cheapest one. No. We compared four factors with the cost per pass. Prompt size, tool count and cache hit rate are not the main cost factors. Steps are. Figure 7. Four factors of each harness and the cost per pass Over the 22 harnesses, the rank correlation of the steps per pass and the cost per pass was +0.51 (p = 0.015). For the other three factors, it was −0.03 to +0.02 (p ≥ 0.88). Within each model, tool calls tracked cost as well as steps. Table 4 below and Table 5 in the appendix give the values. Each step sends the context again, so a trial used 2.0 to 4.8 million input tokens on average, by harness, and the largest first request, 21,365 tokens, is less than 1% of that. mini-SWE-agent has the smallest first request, 882 tokens, but took 38 steps per pass and was 17th of 22 in cost per pass. Over all trials, input from the cache was 42% of the cost, output 33% and other input 25%. The cache makes repeated input much cheaper. Cached input costs 2% (DeepSeek) to 20% (GLM Flash) of the price of other input (Figure 9). Figure 9. List prices of each model (USD for one million tokens) One pair shows the effect of the cache. Cline CLI with DeepSeek (highest cost per task) read 86% of its input from the cache, and OpenCode v1 read 97%. It also sent twice as much input. Input that did not come from the cache was 57% of its cost. 64.5% of the list-price cost of the scored runs went to trials that did not pass : 52.7% to failures and 11.8% to timeouts. The traces of the five best-value harnesses show three common design choices. These are observations, not tests. One shell tool does most of the work. By harness, it got 61% to 93% of the tool calls. Pi’s default prompt has four tools and sends file searches to bash : selectedTools: [...(input.selectedTools ?? ["read", "bash", "edit", "write"])], addRule("Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find"); Each request only adds to the one before it. The start of the context does not change, so the provider reads it from the cache: 91.1% to 94.0% of input in passed trials (Table 4). But 18 of the 22 harnesses read 91% or more, so this does not separate the five. Each step pays the full input price for only about 500 new tokens: # Pi, GLM-5.3, merge-diff-arc-agi-task (trial cd2f6dfd) request prompt tokens cached tokens 8 15,954 15,616 9 16,351 15,936 10 16,999 16,320 No subagents and almost no summaries. Each of the five used a subagent in at most 6 trials, too few to tell if subagents help. Of the five, only Codex CLI summarized, in 8 trials (the 11 Alma trials in Table 6 only drop old images and reminders). Codex CLI summarizes at 90% of the window (Table 6): .map(|context_window| (context_window * 9) / 10); The five also share a weakness. Failed runs end with a confident answer. About three in four failed trials ended with a final answer, not at the time limit: from 68% with Pi to 82% with Codex CLI. Few said that the work was incomplete: # Codex CLI, GLM-5.3, cancel-async-tasks (trial 37182b0e) Agent: - Validated with system Python, including concurrency and cancellation-cleanup tests. Verifier: FAILED test_tasks_cancel_above_max_concurrent assert stdout.count("Cleaned up.") == 2 AssertionError: assert 0 == 2 Trials that did not pass took 60% (Codex CLI) to 69% (Alma) of the cost of each harness.
